items.title: sin(1 degree) is irrational
items.claim: Sine of 30°, 45°, 60° are simple expressions like 1/2, sqrt(2)/2, sqrt(3)/2. Sine of 1 degree, 7 degrees, or most other 'nice' integer degree values are irrational numbers with no closed elementary form.
items.prompt: Why are most integer-degree sine values irrational?

options.text: Niven's theorem (1956): the only rational values of sin(theta) for rational theta in degrees occur at multiples of 30 (giving sin = 0, plus/minus 1/2, plus/minus 1). Almost all other rational-degree sines are irrational

items.reveal_title: Niven's theorem and the gaps in trigonometric tables
items.reveal:
Ivan Niven (1956) proved: if both theta (in degrees) and sin(theta) are rational, then sin(theta) is 0, ±1/2, or ±1. By similar argument, cos(theta) rational with theta rational forces cos(theta) in {0, ±1/2, ±1}.

The consequence: sin(1°), sin(2°), sin(3°), ... are mostly irrational. Specifically, the standard table of integer-degree sines contains only a few rational values: sin(0°) = 0, sin(30°) = 1/2, sin(90°) = 1, and their reflections (150°, 210°, 270°, 330°). Every other entry in the table is irrational.

This is one reason the SPECIAL ANGLES (30°, 45°, 60°) feature so heavily in geometry: they have simple exact values. Most other angles need decimal approximations.

Closed-form expressions: many integer-degree sines do have closed forms in terms of nested radicals — they're algebraic numbers — but the expressions are ugly. For example, sin(15°) = (sqrt(6) - sqrt(2))/4. sin(18°) = (sqrt(5) - 1)/4 (related to the regular pentagon).

For sin(1°): expressible in radicals (it's algebraic, a root of an integer polynomial) but the expression has dozens of nested terms. Modern algebra has tools to compute it exactly; it's just not a useful form.

Why 30° and 45° are special: regular hexagons (60° angles) and squares (45°) tile the plane with simple geometric constructions; the corresponding sine/cosine values come out as simple radicals.

Gauss and constructibility: a regular n-gon is constructible with compass and straightedge if and only if n is a product of powers of 2 and distinct Fermat primes (3, 5, 17, 257, 65537). This is why the 17-gon is constructible (Gauss's first major result, age 19) but the 7-gon and 9-gon aren't.
items.why: Trigonometric tables look like they could be filled with simple values. Almost all entries are deeply irrational, expressible only in nested radicals or numerical approximations. The 'special angles' of school maths are a tiny privileged set.

items.title: The angles of a triangle on a globe don't add to 180 degrees
items.claim: Draw a triangle from the North Pole to the equator at 0 degrees longitude, along the equator to 90 degrees longitude, and back to the North Pole. All three angles are 90 degrees. Total: 270.
items.prompt: How can a triangle have 270 degrees?

options.text: On a curved surface, the angle sum exceeds 180 by an amount proportional to the area enclosed (spherical excess); on a sphere of radius R, sum = 180 + (area / R^2) in radians times 180/pi

items.reveal:
On a flat Euclidean plane, the angles of a triangle sum to exactly 180 degrees.

On a sphere (positive curvature), the sum is more than 180. The excess is proportional to the area: Sum - 180 = (Area / R^2) * (180/pi) for a sphere of radius R. The example triangle (pole-equator-equator-pole) covers 1/8 of the Earth's surface — area ~ 6.4 * 10^7 square km — and has excess 90 degrees.

On a hyperbolic plane (negative curvature), the sum is LESS than 180. The deficit is proportional to area.

This is the deepest test of non-Euclidean geometry: by measuring the angle sum of a triangle, you can tell what kind of space you're in.

Gauss attempted to measure the angle sum of a triangle formed by three mountain peaks (Hohenhagen, Brocken, Inselsberg) in 1820s to test whether space itself is Euclidean. He found no measurable deviation from 180, given his instruments' precision.

General relativity: mass curves space-time. Light follows geodesics through curved space-time. Two photons from a distant source, passing on either side of the Sun, converge (negative curvature in tested region's measurement frame). Detected during the 1919 solar eclipse — confirmation of Einstein.
items.why: Triangles seem to obviously sum to 180. They do on flat surfaces. Real Earth navigation, general relativity, and modern cosmology all use non-Euclidean geometry where triangle sums are observably different.

items.title: 45 degrees is only optimal for a projectile in a vacuum
items.claim: Every physics textbook says the maximum range for a projectile is at launch angle 45 degrees. True in vacuum. In real air, the optimum angle is significantly less — and for some launches it's barely above 30 degrees.
items.prompt: Why does air change the optimum?

options.text: It doesn't — 45 degrees is always optimal
Air resistance reduces both horizontal velocity and vertical velocity, but the loss to drag is greater on long airborne paths; lowering the angle reduces flight time and total drag exposure
Gravity is different at high angles

items.reveal:
Vacuum case: range = (v^2 / g) * sin(2 * theta). Maximised at theta = 45 degrees.

With linear drag (low-speed air): the optimum angle decreases with launch speed and drag coefficient. For a thrown baseball or shot put, optimum is ~42-43 degrees.

With quadratic drag (more realistic at high speed): for a golf ball, optimum is closer to 12-15 degrees (combined with backspin for lift). For an artillery shell, often 30-40 degrees due to high muzzle velocity and dense air.

Why: higher launch angles mean longer flight times, more time exposed to drag, more total energy lost. The trade-off between vertical reach and drag loss shifts the optimum downward.

For a long-jumper, who launches around 7-10 m/s, the optimum angle calculated from biomechanics is ~22 degrees, not 45 — because the long-jumper cannot achieve high vertical velocity from horizontal sprint and because air resistance is minor. Body-mechanics constraints matter more than the equation.

The 45° result is a useful first approximation but should not be taken as universal. Most real-world projectile design uses computational fluid dynamics rather than analytical formulas.
items.why: Textbook results assume ideal conditions. In real applications (golf, baseball, artillery, athletics), the answer is shifted — often substantially — by drag and biomechanical constraints. 'Theoretically 45°' is correct for nothing on Earth.
